title: Bridge and Atlas
premise: In the river city of Vellmora, on the eve of the printers' revolution, Casper Oyelaran works her late father's type cases in a print shop that has quietly become a hub for seditious pamphlets. When a gaunt stranger named Ilse arrives bearing a letter in the unmistakable handwriting of Aldous Vey, the reformist publisher officially executed months ago, Casper realizes the regime staged his death to break the movement — and the letter, naming the officials who ordered it, is the spark that could ignite the city instead. To deliver it to the printers' council beyond the river, Casper and Ilse must carry it past three checkpoints using the one craft the guards never suspect: hidden type, forged passes, and a smuggler's knowledge of what can be carried. Betrayed by the shop's own foreman, hunted as the revolution erupts around them, they lose the letter at the final bridge — and Casper must choose between saving Ilse and setting the type herself, recutting the evidence from memory in the shop of her father's oldest rival, so that on the morning the barricades rise, every handbill in Vellmora carries Vey's living words and the truth of his murder.
about_author: Hazel Ishikawa is a former letterpress apprentice who spent a decade restoring nineteenth-century printing equipment in port towns before turning to fiction. She writes historical novels about the people history forgets to name — the hands that set the type behind great events.

chapters.title: The Weight of Sorts
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. In the Oyelaran print shop, Casper measures her world in ems and picas, hiding pamphlet plates among her father's funeral type. The foreman, Doss, watches her too closely. Emotional beat: quiet defiance and grief for a father who taught her that letters outlive men.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Ink Door
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Ilse Vey arrives soaked from the river, carrying a sealed letter she claims is from her executed brother. Casper recognizes the handwriting from proofs she once set. Emotional beat: the shock of the impossible, and the first pull of belonging to something larger.

chapters.title: What the Corpse Wrote
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Ilse explains how she smuggled the letter out of the prison records office; the letter names three ministers who ordered Vey's staged execution. Casper tests the hand against old type specimens and it matches. Emotional beat: dread hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Foreman's Silence
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Doss offers to help — too readily — and Casper lies to him about the letter's contents while hiding it inside a font case of broken sorts. Emotional beat: the loneliness of trust rationed like ink.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. They map the route to the printers' council across the river: the Customs House, the Garrison Arch, and the Bridge of Atlas, where soldiers weigh every cart. Emotional beat: fear made concrete, a plan drawn in pencil that can be erased.

chapters.title: The Type That Lies
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Casper forges a customs pass using a discarded official font, and the two rehearse their cover as type merchants delivering a consignment. Emotional beat: the strange intimacy of two women building a lie together.

chapters.title: Customs House
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. First checkpoint: a clerk who collects confiscated books, nearly undone by his hunger to touch their 'specimen book.' Ilse flatters his obsession while the letter sits in plain sight as a printer's proof. Emotional beat: terror transmuted into performance.

chapters.title: The Pamphlet Riots
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Back in the city, riots ignite over a bread levy; the shop is raided while they're away, and Doss covers for them — at a price. Emotional beat: guilt, and the first hint that Doss is playing his own game.

chapters.title: Garrison Arch
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Second checkpoint: a captain who knew Aldous Vey and looks too long at Ilse's face, which mirrors her brother's. She talks her way through by claiming to be a stranger to her own name. Emotional beat: the cost of survival is erasing yourself.

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Waiting in a safehouse, Casper sorts through her father's old kit and remembers fleeing a pogrom as a child with only a type case on her back. Emotional beat: the theme made flesh — a life measured in what fits in your hands.

chapters.title: The Council That Waits
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. They reach the printers' council's contact, a blind compositor named Merrick, who reveals the council is paralyzed by fear and will only act on the letter if delivered publicly, at the Bridge of Atlas, during the levy protests. Emotional beat: hope curdling into a harder task.

chapters.title: Doss's Price
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Doss demands the shop and Casper's silence in exchange for hiding Merrick; she realizes he has been reporting to the ministers all along. Emotional beat: betrayal as revelation — the trap was built from inside.

chapters.title: The Broken Font
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Ilse goes back for a second letter — Vey's full testimony — and finds the prison records office burning, the regime destroying its own evidence. She escapes with scorched pages. Emotional beat: desperation; history being erased faster than it can be carried.

chapters.title: Hunted Through the Paper District
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Soldiers with Doss's descriptions sweep the print quarter; Casper and Ilse flee across rooftops of drying paper, the city's pamphlets fluttering like birds. Emotional beat: the revolution arriving as chaos they can no longer steer.

chapters.title: The Bridge of Atlas
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Third checkpoint: the bridge itself, jammed with fleeing crowds. The letter is seized in a search; Ilse is taken while Casper escapes downstream. Emotional beat: the arc's lowest point — everything carried, lost.

chapters.title: Recut from Memory
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Casper turns to her father's rival, old Sef Brandt, and together they recut Vey's letter from Casper's memory of the proofs, letter by letter, through the night. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into craft; the dead man's voice rebuilt by hand.

chapters.title: The Printers Rise
chapters.summary: Casper and Ilse's alternating POV. At dawn the presses run in a dozen shops at once; the city wakes to ten thousand copies of Vey's testimony. Ilse, escaped during the mob's surge, finds Casper ink-stained and shaking. Emotional beat: the climax — words as the true weapon.

chapters.title: Doss at the Door
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Doss comes to burn the shop and the plates; Merrick and the apprentices stand him off, and Casper chooses not to kill him, locking him in the type vault instead. Emotional beat: power offered and refused — the theme answered.

chapters.title: The Fall of the Ministers
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. The named ministers flee as the garrison refuses orders; Vey, alive in hiding, emerges to a city that already believes him. Ilse declines a place at his side. Emotional beat: victory that costs the victors their old lives.

chapters.title: What the Fire Took
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Casper surveys the ruined shop, salvages her father's original type case, and buries Doss's confiscated plates in the river. Emotional beat: mourning and accounting — what survival has cost her.

chapters.title: A New Face of Type
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Casper and Ilse reopen the shop as a cooperative press, cutting a new typeface they name Atlas. The first job is a school primer, not a pamphlet. Emotional beat: belonging found not in a cause but in a craft shared.

chapters.title: The Letters Outlive Us
chapters.summary: Casper's POV, years later. An apprentice asks Casper why she measures everything in ems; she answers with the story's thesis — that power is what can be seized, but truth is what can be carried. Final image: the presses running as the city celebrates the anniversary of the rising. Emotional beat: resolution, legacy, and peace.
